stops.name: Château d'Oex, the commandant draws mandalas
stops.campa: Called up as commandant of the British interned soldiers at Château d'Oex in the Vaud Alps, Jung rises each morning and sketches in a notebook a small circular drawing, a mandala, which corresponds to his inner situation of that day, and watches the circles correct him, rebuke him, restore him. Here he grasps what the years of descent were seeking: the goal is not a line but a centre; the self is the circumference and the midpoint; all paths are circumambulations. The war ends around him while the commandant of the interned discovers the geometry of the soul.
stops.quote: I sketched every morning in a notebook a small circular drawing, a mandala, which seemed to correspond to my inner situation at the time.

stops.name: Algiers, Europe seen from outside
stops.campa: Jung lands at Algiers in the March light, his first step off the European shelf. The muezzin's cry, the white city stacked against the hill, the unhurried crowds: time itself runs at another pace here, and he feels the centuries fall away like coats. What Europe calls Oriental apathy he reads at once as a different relation of the ego to the sun. He has come, he realizes, not to study the Arab but to catch sight of the European, himself, from a point outside, and the sight is not flattering.

stops.name: Tunis, the older time
stops.campa: In the medina of Tunis Jung walks for hours without a plan, letting the souks close over him. Here is a civilization layered like his Atlantic dream-house: French officialdom on top, then the Ottoman, the Arab, the Roman, Carthage under everything and the desert under Carthage. He feels the emotional tug of this world on some stratum of himself that Europe has paved over, and feels too a subtle danger, as of a man leaning over dark water. The unconscious, he notes, takes the features of whatever older world one enters.

stops.name: Sousse, the dream of the Arab prince
stops.campa: At Sousse, within the walls above the harbour, the answering dream comes. A young Arab prince, proud and handsome, attacks Jung on a bridge before a casbah, wrestles him, and tries to force his head under the water, to drown him, not quite to kill him, and then, in a vaulted chamber, is made to read Jung's own book. Waking, Jung understands: the dusky one is the shadow-royalty of his own soul, the self that Europe humiliates, which would rather drown the thinker than be unread. He carries the prince home with him, an ambassador accredited for life.

stops.name: Küsnacht, the mother dies; Wotan rides
stops.campa: Emilie Preiswerk-Jung dies suddenly in January. The night before the news reaches him, Jung dreams he stands in a dense, dark wood among gigantic primeval trees, and hears a wolf-howl and the shattering call of Wotan's wild hunt sweeping the sky: the Hunter come to fetch a soul of his own kin. He travels home through the night, and grief runs in him side by side with an incomprehensible undertone of the marriage-dance of the dead. The night-mother of the parsonage, the two-voiced priestess, is gathered to the older god she always half served.

stops.name: Bollingen, the Tower begun with his own hands
stops.campa: Two months after his mother's death Jung begins to build at Bollingen, on the reed-fringed shore of the upper lake he loved as a student: land bought from the church of St. Meinrad, old cloister ground. He learns to split stone from the Bollingen quarrymen and lays courses with his own hands. Words and paper are not real enough: the tower is his confession of faith in stone, round like the maternal hearth, without electricity or pipe-water, where the dead of the family may come to the fire and the twentieth century must wait outside on the road.
stops.quote: Words and paper, however, did not seem real enough to me; something more was needed. I had to make a confession of faith in stone. That was the beginning of the 'Tower.'

stops.name: Taos Pueblo, Mountain Lake speaks
stops.campa: On the roof of the adobe town under Taos Mountain, in the thin January sun, Jung sits wrapped in a blanket beside Ochwiay Biano, Mountain Lake, of the sun-keeping people. The Pueblo man says the whites are always seeking, their faces cruel and furrowed, and that the Indians think them mad. Jung asks why mad. Because they say they think with their heads. And what do you think with? We think here, says Mountain Lake, touching his heart. For the first time in his life, Jung records, someone has drawn for him the portrait of the real white man, and it strikes like a spear.
stops.quote: 'We think that they are mad.' I asked him why he thought the whites were all mad. 'They say that they think with their heads,' he replied. 'Why of course. What do you think with?' I asked him in surprise. 'We think here,' he said, indicating his heart.

stops.name: Mombasa, landfall of the Bugishu Psychological Expedition
stops.campa: Having sailed from Southampton on 15 October with Baynes and Beckwith, joined on the boat by Ruth Bailey, foretold as the fourth, Jung lands at Mombasa, humid, half-Arab, hung with mangoes and old Portuguese guns. The expedition carries a name half in jest, the Bugishu Psychological Expedition, and a purpose wholly serious: to find the psyche before Europe touched it. They take the night train inland, and Africa begins to burn away the doctor of Küsnacht layer by layer, like the label off a bottle in the rain.

stops.name: The Uganda railway, the man on the rock: five thousand years home
stops.campa: At first light the train curves along a red cliff, and above the carriage, motionless on a jag of rock, stands a slim black figure leaning on a long spear, gazing down. Jung is transfixed by the most intense sentiment du déjà vu of his life: he knows this man; he has known this moment always; he is not arriving in a foreign land but returning, after five thousand years, to the country of his youth. The railway rattles on toward Nairobi carrying a European who has just remembered something older than Europe.
stops.quote: I had the feeling that I had already experienced this moment and had always known this world.

stops.name: Athi Plains, the man who completes creation
stops.campa: From a low hill on the Athi Plains outside Nairobi, Jung looks out over gigantic herds of gazelle, antelope, gnu, zebra and warthog grazing and moving like slow rivers to the horizon, in a stillness that is the eternal beginning, the world as it was before anyone knew it was a world. His companions fade from his sight. Here the cosmic meaning of consciousness is given to him whole: in an invisible act of creation, man puts the stamp of perfection on the world by knowing it. The unknowing world sinks; the knower stands; the second cosmogony is accomplished on a hill in Kenya.
stops.quote: There the cosmic meaning of consciousness became overwhelmingly clear to me... Man, I, in an invisible act of creation put the stamp of perfection on the world by giving it objective existence.

stops.name: Mount Elgon, among the Elgonyi
stops.campa: The expedition camps at 7,000 feet on the slopes of Mount Elgon, the extinct volcano on the Uganda border, among the Elgonyi in their kraals. Under an old chief's courtesy Jung holds palavers on dreams and learns a hard news: since the English came, the big dreams have ceased: the District Commissioner now knows the future that the medicine-man once dreamed. The laibon says it with tears in his eyes. Jung writes it down like a man recording the extinction of a species: the dreaming office of mankind, resigning.

stops.name: Mount Elgon, the dawn worship: adhista
stops.campa: Each morning Jung leaves his tent to watch the sun come up over the Elgon forests, when the light unfolds like a polyphony and the world becomes for an instant so glorious that it hurts. The Elgonyi show him their only rite: at the moment the sun rises they spit on their hands and hold the palms to the first light, or breathe on them: offering to the risen god the living substance of the soul. Not the sun itself is God, the elders agree, but the moment of its rising: adhista. Jung recognizes the oldest prayer of mankind, and joins it privately for the rest of his life.
stops.quote: The sunrise in these latitudes was a phenomenon that overwhelmed me anew every day.
